---
title: "Tutorial: block averages and totals of a continuous map"
execute:
  warning: false
---

This tutorial works through the eight steps of Wadoux & Heuvelink (2023, Section 4.1) on
the synthetic example from the authors' R script:

- a 100 × 100 grid on [0, 100]²;
- a linear trend plus a Gaussian random field with covariance 5·exp(−h/25);
- 200 sample points;
- a 250-tree quantile regression forest on the coordinates, with 10-fold
  cross-validation.

The last section repeats the aggregation on the R script's own exported outputs and
compares the numbers with R.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup and plotting style"
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import pyspatialuncertainty as psu
from pyspatialuncertainty.synthetic import PipelineScenario

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb",
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
                     "axes.edgecolor": "#c9c8c2", "axes.titlesize": 10, "font.size": 9})
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, YELLOW = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100"
```

## Steps 1–2: point predictions and their uncertainty

`PipelineScenario` re-implements the R script: it simulates the field, samples it,
cross-validates a ranger-style quantile regression forest and maps it. The forest
predicts at each location a conditional distribution, summarised as 500 draws. Their mean
is the prediction and their standard deviation is σ(s) (step 2). If your model returns
samples or quantiles instead, `psu.sd_from_samples` and `psu.sd_from_quantiles` compute σ.

```{python}
scenario = PipelineScenario()            # the R script's settings
real = scenario.simulate(np.random.default_rng(31415))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.2), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (da, title) in zip(axes, [(real.truth, "Truth"), (real.prediction, "QRF prediction"),
                                  (real.sd, "Prediction-error SD σ(s)")]):
    im = ax.imshow(da.values, origin="lower", extent=(0, 100, 0, 100), cmap="viridis")
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
v = real.validation
axes[0].scatter(v["x"], v["y"], s=4, c="white", edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.3)
plt.show()
```

## Step 3: standardized cross-validation errors

The predictions and σ at the sample points come from the cross-validation folds, so no
model ever predicted a point it was trained on.

```{python}
val = psu.standardized_errors(v, observed="observed", predicted="predicted", sd="sd")
val.select("x", "y", "observed", "predicted", "sd", "std_error").head()
```

## Step 4: correlation of the standardized errors

`fit_correlation` fits a nugget plus an exponential, spherical or Gaussian structure to
the standardized errors by Gaussian maximum likelihood. By default the mean of the errors
is fixed at zero, as unbiased predictions imply. A common offset of the validation errors
then counts as evidence of long-range correlation, which matters most for large blocks.

The paper fits a sample variogram by weighted least squares instead. That is
`method="wls"`: a gstat-style sample variogram (a cutoff of 0.33333 × the bounding-box
diagonal and 15 lag classes) with gstat's `fit.method = 7`, as in the R script. Both
results carry the sample variogram, for checking the fit visually.

```{python}
fit = psu.fit_correlation(val)
wls = psu.fit_correlation(val, method="wls")
ev = fit.empirical
print(fit.model)
print(f"variance of the standardized errors: {val['std_error'].var():.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Sample variogram of the standardized CV errors (dots, sized by number of pairs), the likelihood fit (default) and the paper's WLS fit."
h = np.linspace(0, ev.cutoff, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.scatter(ev.dist, ev.gamma, s=ev.n_pairs / 10, color=BLUE, zorder=3)
ax.plot(h[1:], fit.model.gamma(h[1:]), color=BLUE, label="likelihood (default)")
ax.plot(h[1:], wls.model.gamma(h[1:]), color=ORANGE, ls="--", label="WLS (paper)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
ax.axhline(1.0, color="#8a8984", lw=1, ls="--")
ax.annotate("sill expected if σ is calibrated", (ev.cutoff, 1.0), ha="right", va="bottom", color="#52514e")
ax.set_xlabel("distance"); ax.set_ylabel("semivariance"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.15)
plt.show()
```

The fitted sill is the variance of the standardized errors. **A sill well below 1 means
the forest's σ is too wide.** In the R script the hand-set model has a sill of 0.65, and
this realization tells the same story.

The paper converts the variogram into a correlogram, ρ(h) = (sill − γ(h))/sill. That
keeps only the *shape* of the correlation and trusts σ for the *scale*, so any error in σ
passes straight into the block standard deviations. The package keeps this faithful
behaviour. Check the sill before you interpret the results.

```{python}
rho = fit.model.to_correlation()
print("rho at h = 0, 1, 5, 20:", np.round(rho(np.array([0.0, 1, 5, 20])), 3))
```

## Steps 5–8: Monte Carlo integration over blocks

The blocks are the whole domain (the box [0, 100]² used in the R script) and 25 × 25 tiles.
For each block, `aggregate_continuous` draws 10,000 pairs of uniform points, averages
σ(s)σ(u)ρ(|s − u|), and reports four things:

- the SD of the block average, with its Monte Carlo standard error;
- the SD of the block total, which is |B| times the SD of the average;
- normal prediction intervals;
- the relative error.

```{python}
domain = psu.aggregate_continuous(real.sd, fit.model, psu.blocks.box(0, 0, 100, 100, real.sd),
                                  prediction=real.prediction, n_mc=10_000, level=0.90, seed=1)
domain.table.select("mean_pred", "sd_mean", "mcse_sd", "lower", "upper", "total_pred", "sd_total")
```

```{python}
print(f"true block mean {float(real.truth.mean()):.3f}; prediction {domain.table['mean_pred'][0]:.3f}")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Large blocks depend on the tail of the correlogram

For the whole domain, the variance of the block mean depends mostly on the weak,
long-range part of the correlation. A short-range model that fits the first few lag
classes well can miss it. The R script's hand-set model has a nugget, a short exponential
structure, and weak spherical (range 15) and exponential (range 60) structures. Below, the
same nested model is fitted to this realization's sample variogram, with the ranges held
fixed and only the sills fitted, and compared with the likelihood fit and the paper's
automatic WLS fit.
:::

```{python}
nested_start = (psu.vgm(0.46, "Exp", 2, nugget=0.05) + psu.vgm(0.08, "Sph", 15)
                + psu.vgm(0.06, "Exp", 60))
nested = psu.fit_variogram(ev, nested_start, fit_ranges=False)
print(nested.model)
dom_nested = psu.aggregate_continuous(real.sd, nested.model, psu.blocks.box(0, 0, 100, 100, real.sd),
                                      prediction=real.prediction, n_mc=10_000, seed=1)
dom_wls = psu.aggregate_continuous(real.sd, wls.model, psu.blocks.box(0, 0, 100, 100, real.sd),
                                   prediction=real.prediction, n_mc=10_000, seed=1)
results = [domain, dom_wls, dom_nested]
pl.DataFrame({"correlogram": ["likelihood fit (default)", "WLS fit (paper)", "nested, R-script ranges"],
              "sd_of_domain_mean": [r.table["sd_mean"][0] for r in results],
              "mcse_sd": [r.table["mcse_sd"][0] for r in results]})
```

In this realization the error of the domain mean,
`{python} f"{float(real.truth.mean()) - domain.table['mean_pred'][0]:.3f}"`, is
`{python} f"{abs(float(real.truth.mean()) - domain.table['mean_pred'][0]) / domain.table['sd_mean'][0]:.1f}"`
standard deviations under the likelihood fit,
`{python} f"{abs(float(real.truth.mean()) - domain.table['mean_pred'][0]) / dom_wls.table['sd_mean'][0]:.1f}"`
under the WLS fit and
`{python} f"{abs(float(real.truth.mean()) - domain.table['mean_pred'][0]) / dom_nested.table['sd_mean'][0]:.1f}"`
under the nested fit. The [verification report](../report.html) quantifies the effect of
the correlogram tail across many realizations, and `experiments/improvements/` in the
repository compares the likelihood and WLS fits.

```{python}
tiles = psu.aggregate_continuous(real.sd, fit.model, psu.blocks.tiles(real.sd, 25),
                                 prediction=real.prediction, n_mc=10_000, seed=2)
coarse = tiles.to_xarray(coarse=True)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.4), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, var, title in [(axes[0], "mean_pred", "Block mean prediction"), (axes[1], "sd_mean", "SD of block mean")]:
    im = ax.imshow(coarse[var].values, origin="lower", extent=(0, 100, 0, 100), cmap="viridis")
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
plt.show()
```

## Naive alternatives

The paper warns against two shortcuts. Averaging the point SDs assumes perfectly
correlated errors. Treating cells as independent gives sqrt(Σσ²)/n. On this map they
bracket the correct answer by a wide margin:

```{python}
grid = psu.GridSpec.from_dataarray(real.sd)
sdv = grid.values(real.sd)
rb = psu.resolve_blocks(psu.blocks.box(0, 0, 100, 100, grid), np.isfinite(sdv))
pl.DataFrame({
    "approach": ["Monte Carlo integration (this method)", "average of point SDs", "independent errors"],
    "sd_of_block_mean": [domain.table["sd_mean"][0], psu.sd_average(rb, sdv)[0], psu.sd_independent(rb, sdv)[0]],
})
```

## Reproducing the authors' R results

The repository ships the R script's exported intermediates in `tests/data/r_reference`:
the map, the QRF predictions and variances, the hand-set variogram model, and the exact
Monte Carlo pairs the script drew. Here they go through the same function.

```{python}
import xarray as xr
from pathlib import Path

ref = next(d / "tests/data/r_reference" for d in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]
           if (d / "tests/data/r_reference").exists())
rd = lambda name: pl.read_csv(ref / name, infer_schema_length=None)
g = rd("grid.csv")
c = np.sort(g["x1"].unique().to_numpy())
as_da = lambda col: xr.DataArray(g[col].to_numpy().reshape(100, 100), coords={"y": c, "x": c}, dims=("y", "x"))
model_r = psu.VariogramModel.from_table(rd("variogram_model.csv"))
print(model_r)

res_r = psu.aggregate_continuous(np.sqrt(as_da("predVarRF")), model_r, psu.blocks.box(0, 0, 100, 100, as_da("y")),
                                 prediction=as_da("predRF"), n_mc=1_000_000, z=1.64, seed=1)
summary = dict(zip(*rd("summary.csv").to_dict(as_series=False).values()))
pl.DataFrame({
    "quantity": ["SD of block mean", "90% PI lower (z = 1.64)", "90% PI upper", "SD of block total"],
    "R script (m = 1,000)": [summary["sd_average"], summary["pi90_lower_z164"], summary["pi90_upper_z164"], summary["sd_total"]],
    "Python (m = 1,000,000)": [res_r.table["sd_mean"][0], res_r.table["lower"][0], res_r.table["upper"][0], res_r.table["sd_total"][0]],
})
```

The two estimates differ by about one Monte Carlo standard error of the R script's
1,000-pair estimate (MCSE of the variance: `{python} f"{summary['mcse_script']:.4f}"`).
The test suite also shows that the integrand matches R to machine precision on the
script's own point pairs. The [verification report](../report.html) has the full parity
study, along with coverage results across many realizations.
